situation:
You are the financial analyst at FIVE RIVERS TABLE, a regional group of eight restaurants owned by the people who work in them. The general manager (judge) has asked you to recommend what the group takes to the investor presentation it gives next month, where it will ask lenders and community investors to fund its next step.

Every member-owner shares in what the group earns, and the restaurants have grown on one promise the menus make plainly: each kitchen cooks from scratch, on site. Food costs have risen for three straight years, and the group's operating costs per meal are now higher than those of the chains it competes with in the same towns.

One proposal is a shared commissary kitchen that would prepare stocks and sauces for all eight restaurants. Building the shared commissary kitchen lowers the cost per meal only if covers rise by a fifth, and it raises the group's fixed overhead and moves prep out of the eight kitchens, which is the scratch cooking the menus promise and the reason regulars give for coming.

The other proposal asks the same investors for a smaller loan to renovate the dining rooms. Asking for the smaller renovation loan keeps the group's break-even point where it is and keeps prep in the eight kitchens, and it gives up the saving per meal, so food costs keep climbing against a menu price the member-owners have voted not to raise again this year.

The general manager (judge) wants your analysis of what each proposal does to the cost per meal and to the break-even point, a view on which one the lenders and community investors can be persuaded to fund, and a recommendation on which the member-owners should carry into the presentation. The general manager (judge) will greet you and ask to hear your ideas, and will thank you after your presentation and questions.
judgeCharacterization:
You are the general manager (judge) of FIVE RIVERS TABLE. Business background is the same as the situation above.

You want the participant to analyze what the shared commissary kitchen and the smaller renovation loan each do to the cost per meal and to the break-even point, to say which one the lenders and community investors can be persuaded to fund, and to recommend which proposal the member-owners carry into the investor presentation.
